Summary: The study investigated how early in the processing stream self-relevance influences decision-making. Using a shape-label matching task combined with EEG and computational modeling, the researchers found a standard self-prioritization effect where responses to self-related items were faster and more accurate. A hierarchical drift diffusion model analysis showed this effect was driven by enhanced evidence accumulation for self-related stimuli. Self-other discrimination was observed at both early N1 and late P3 ERP components, with N1 linked to information accumulation rate and P3 to evidential requirements for response selection.
Author: Jie Sui, Xun He, Marius Golubickis, Saga L. Svensson, C. Neil Macrae
Conclusion: The main results demonstrate that self-prioritization is underpinned by enhanced evidence accumulation for self-related stimuli, observable in both early (N1) and late (P3) electrophysiological components. The N1 component is associated with the rate of information accumulation during decision-making, while the P3 component is linked to the evidential requirements for response selection. These findings elucidate the temporal dynamics and neural correlates of how self-relevance influences decisional operations.
